https://macworld.com/article/672537/when.html:
Macworld

Apple announced HomeView, HomePod mini 2, a new Apple TV 4K and the Apple Home Collection at its “Welcome Home” launch on October 13, 2026. But that will not be its final announcements this month.

Apple has reportedly invited selected media to another product launch experience, this time in Los Angeles on Wednesday October 28. That new date is a day after the date reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman, who initially reported that another launch was planned for October 27. The product launch could still take place on the 27 October though.

Apple is expected to reveal a touchscreen MacBooks, an M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, an M6 iMac and an OLED iPad mini and these are likely to be the products being showcased at the media event.

Apple typically has four main event windows each year: a spring event, WWDC in June, the iPhone event in September, and sometimes a further event in October. The company rarely confirms dates far in advance, and there’s no guarantee it will hold an event in every window. That leaves Apple fans – and anyone considering a new Apple device – wondering when the next event will happen and what might be announced. Fortunately, Apple’s annual schedule is fairly predictable, while reliable rumours often provide additional clues about what’s coming. That means we can make informed estimates about the timing of future keynotes and the products most likely to appear.Here’s everything we know about the next event Apple will hold – and beyond.

When is Apple’s next event?

  • October 28, 2026: Apple is said to be inviting select media to a product launch event.

Apple has invited some media to a product launch experience on October 28 in Los Angeles. The next launch may still take place on October 27, 2026, the date initially reported by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

Gurman previously said the launch will include a video presentation and a gathering for journalists. Apple held a “Welcome Home” experience for select media on October 13. In March, it also hosted an “Apple Experience” alongside three days of product announcements. Those launches suggest a possible model for late October.

What could Apple launch at the next event?

Apple is expected to unveil its long-rumored touchscreen MacBook Pro, a 14-inch MacBook Pro with an M6 chip, an M6 iMac and an OLED iPad mini at the reported October 27 or 28 launch.

Apple event calendar 2026: What has Apple launched this year?

Apple has held four events so far in 2026, including its March and October hands-on Experiences. On March 4, the company invited select media to hands-on “experiences” in multiple locations. In the run-up to that date, Apple launched several products via press release, including the iPhone 17e, M4 iPad Air, and M5 Pro and M5 Max MacBook Pro, M5 MacBook Air and the MacBook Neo.

The second event was WWDC, which began with a keynote on June 8. At the WWDC keynote Apple outlined the upcoming changes to its operating systems, including iOS 27 and macOS 27 Golden Gate.

In August Apple issued press releases to announce the new Mac mini and Mac Studio.

At the September 9 event Apple unveiled the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, a foldable iPhone Duo, a new Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4, and AirPods 5.

Apple’s October 13 “Welcome Home” announcements included HomeView, a new smart-home display with a 7-inch touchscreen; HomePod mini 2; a fourth-generation Apple TV 4K with an updated Siri Remote; and the Apple Home Collection, a range of cameras, doorbells, locks, and thermostats developed with accessory partners.

Foundry

FAQ

1.

How far in advance does Apple announce an event?

Apple usually announces its events around one to two weeks before they take place, although the timing varies. The October 13, 2026 Experience was announced just five days in advance. Apple also sometimes chooses to announce products via press release without holding an event.

2.

How long is an Apple keynote?

Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature the CEO alongside various other Apple executives.

WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter.

For example, the September 2024 event was 1 hour 38 minutes.

3.

What time do Apple events normally start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones?

Apple’s events tend to start at 10 am PT or 1 pm ET. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:

  • U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
  • Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
  • U.K.: 6 pm
  • Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
  • India: 10:30 pm IST
  • Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
  • New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST

The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere (in 2026 the clocks will change in the U.S. on November 1, while in the U.K. they change on October 25).

Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. The event on October 13, 2026 started at 9 am in New York, 2 pm in the U.K.

If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release, that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.

4.

How often does Apple hold events?

There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:

  • Spring Event
  • WWDC in June
  • iPhone Event in September
  • Late Fall Event in October

This event calendar is by no means set in stone, though, with the spring and October events being less regular. Some years, Apple doesn’t hold a spring event at all. In 2025 Apple only held two events, preferring instead to announce new products via press release.

5.

Will there be a live stream at the next Apple Event?

There was no public livestream for the October 13 Experience and one isn’t expected for the rumored October 27 or 28 event.

Apple usually livestreams the iPhone announcement in September and the WWDC keynote in June.

6.

Does Apple ever announce products without an event?

Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. In recent years, the company has increasingly reserved its large-scale media events for major flagship launches, such as the primary iPhone lineup in September, while using press releases for iterative updates or “chip bumps” that may not warrant a full hour-long presentation.

7.

How to watch an Apple event

Apple events are typically broadcast across several digital platforms, allowing viewers to tune in from almost any device. While the company previously restricted access to its own hardware or the Safari browser, these barriers have been removed in recent years.

FAQ

1.

How far in advance does Apple announce an event?

Apple usually announces its events around one to two weeks before they take place, although the timing varies. The October 13, 2026 Experience was announced just five days in advance. Apple also sometimes chooses to announce products via press release without holding an event.

2.

How long is an Apple keynote?

Apple keynotes usually last between one and two hours and feature the CEO alongside various other Apple executives.

WWDC and the September event tend to be longer keynotes; the spring and late-fall events can be slightly shorter.

For example, the September 2024 event was 1 hour 38 minutes.

3.

What time do Apple events normally start in U.S., U.K. and other global time zones?

Apple’s events tend to start at 10 am PT or 1 pm ET. That translates to the following times in the countries where most of our readers live:

  • U.S.: 10 am PDT, 11 am MDT, 12 pm CDT, 1 pm EDT
  • Canada: as above, plus 2 pm ADT
  • U.K.: 6 pm
  • Europe: 7 pm CEST, 8 pm EEST
  • India: 10:30 pm IST
  • Australia: next day — 1 am AWST, 2:30 am ACST, 3 am AEST
  • New Zealand: next day — 5 am NZST

The timings are generally the same for all Apple Keynotes, but can be slightly different if Apple holds the event during the period of a couple of weeks when the clocks have changed in the U.S. but not elsewhere (in 2026 the clocks will change in the U.S. on November 1, while in the U.K. they change on October 25).

Sometimes Apple holds events at different times, for example, in October 2023 the event was held in late afternoon in San Francisco, which meant it was midnight in the U.K. The event on October 13, 2026 started at 9 am in New York, 2 pm in the U.K.

If Apple doesn’t hold an event and instead just issues a press release, that usually happens around 8 am PT, 11 am ET and 4 pm U.K. time.

There can be as many as four Apple events in a year:

  • Spring Event

There was no public livestream for the October 13 Experience and one isn’t expected for the rumored October 27 or 28 event.

Apple usually livestreams the iPhone announcement in September and the WWDC keynote in June.

Apple frequently announces products without a keynote event, often opting for press releases or multi-day announcement windows. The touchscreen MacBook is reportedly going to be a reality very soon (October 28, apparently), and one of the questions about the new way to interface with the Mac is how macOS will accommodate our fingers. According to some clues in the latest beta, we can get an idea of what Apple is planning.

A post by itspdfu points out that Safari in the macOS beta has new UI elements designed for touch input. When rearranging tabs, the tab “lifts” and then enlarges as you drag it to the new location, then goes back to its original size when you drop it. Tabs don’t currently operate like this when you click and drag using a mouse or trackpad.

Also, you can tap and hold a tab to open the context menu, but it doesn’t show an Ask Siri option as it does with a mouse or trackpad–I’m not sure why Apple removed it. It’s also hard to tell from the screen capture whether the contextual menu options are slightly larger to make them easier to tap.

But it’s clear that Apple is rethinking how we interact with macOS ahead of a big interface chance. We expect the new MacBook will ship with macOS 27.2 preinstalled when it arrives.

Itsdpfu, who has a reputation of accurate leaks, also said their post is “part 1” so stay tuned for more.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro has been the subject of speculation ever since Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman first reported in 2023 that Apple was exploring the idea. At the time, the claim seemed hard to believe given Apple’s long-standing opposition to touchscreen laptops. Three years later, however, the rumours are becoming increasingly difficult to dismiss.

Multiple reports suggest Apple has overcome the technical and design challenges that previously stood in the way. If they’re accurate, the first touchscreen MacBook Pro will arrive as part of one of the biggest redesigns in the laptop’s history, combining a new chassis with Apple’s first OLED MacBook display and potentially even an iPhone-style Dynamic Island camera cutout.

The timing would be fitting. The MacBook Pro celebrates its 20th anniversary in 2026, and Apple could mark the milestone with a feature many believed would never come to the Mac. Touchscreen support would also help further differentiate the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the budget-friendly MacBook Neo.

There are still questions over pricing. OLED panels and ongoing supply-chain pressures are expected to make the new models more expensive than today’s MacBook Pro. Apple is also expected to keep touchscreen technology exclusive to its premium laptops initially, with no indication that it will come to the MacBook Air or MacBook Neo in the first generation. Read on for a complete roundup of the latest touchscreen MacBook Pro rumours, including what the most reliable sources are saying, how credible each report is, and what we think Apple is likely to announce and when.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro release date: When will it launch?

  • Expected announcement: October 27, 2026, shipping on November 6, 2026, according to Bloomberg

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman reported on October 8 that Apple plans to announce its first touchscreen MacBook on October 27. The launch will reportedly include an online video presentation and an in-person component for the press on October 28. In his Power On podcast, Gurman said the laptop will start shipping on November 6.

Earlier reports offered a broader launch window and raised the possibility of delays. Speaking in a Power On podcast on October 1, Gurman said he expected the touchscreen MacBook announcement as early as October, potentially slipping to November. The laptops are reportedly being tested with macOS 27.2.

In September 2026, Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman included the touchscreen MacBooks in a list of products that will ship in late 2026/early 2027.

Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo both initially predicted a late 2026 debut, with an October announcement fitting Apple’s traditional MacBook Pro release schedule while also coinciding with the 20th anniversary of the MacBook Pro’s introduction. In January, South Korean blog Naver reported that Samsung had begun production on its new 8.6-generation OLED manufacturing line, which is expected to supply panels for the next-generation MacBook Pro, further supporting that timeframe. Gurman also reported in February that the redesigned MacBook Pro would arrive in the “back half” of 2026.

However, the launch could still slip to early 2027. Global DRAM and NAND shortages, which prompted Apple to raise Mac and iPad prices in June 2026 – are expected to continue well into 2027. In April, Gurman reported that supply-chain constraints were affecting development of the redesigned MacBook Pro and could push the release into early 2027. He subsequently reported in June that Apple had revised its chip roadmap, with the touchscreen MacBook Pro now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max chips instead of M6 Pro and M6 Max in an effort to keep the project on schedule. In a July report, Gurman reiterated that these laptops are planned for this fall, but a 2027 ship date is possible.

Which MacBook models will get a touchscreen?

  • Current rumours suggest that Apple’s first touchscreen laptop will be a redesigned MacBook Pro with Pro and Max chips

Both Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman and analyst Ming-Chi Kuo have reported that Apple is developing MacBook Pro models with OLED touchscreen displays as part of a major redesign. The feature is expected to debut on the high-end MacBook Pro models powered by Apple’s Pro and Max chips, making them the first Macs to support direct touch input.

Apple is expected to use the touchscreen as a key differentiator for its professional laptops, further separating the MacBook Pro from the more affordable MacBook Air and MacBook Neo.

There is also speculation that Apple could rebrand the flagship model as the MacBook Ultra. According to one report from a source said to be familiar with Apple’s plans, the company intends to expand its “Ultra” branding beyond the Mac Studio and Apple silicon chips. However, this claim has not been corroborated by Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman or analyst Ming-Chi Kuo, so it should be treated with caution.

For now, the technology appears set to remain exclusive to the MacBook Pro lineup. Neither the MacBook Air nor the MacBook Neo is expected to gain touchscreen support in the near term. However, Kuo believes Apple could eventually expand the technology to other MacBook models if the touchscreen MacBook Pro proves successful.

The MacBook Air may be the next candidate for a touchscreen upgrade, but current forecasts suggest this is unlikely before 2028 or 2029. Some reports also indicate that the Air could adopt OLED display technology before then, albeit without touch functionality.

Touchscreen MacBook Pro Design

  • Lighter design expected
  • Punch hole for the FaceTime camera

Apple’s touchscreen MacBook Pro is expected to have a substantially lighter design than current models, but it may not be significantly thinner. Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman has revised his earlier expectations for a slimmer body while maintaining that Apple has redesigned and consolidated internal components to reduce weight.

One of the most significant visual changes could be the removal of the display notch. Reports from display analysts and Bloomberg suggest Apple may replace the current notch with a hole-punch camera cutout, allowing for more usable screen space around the sensor. In early 2026, Gurman went a step further, claiming the new MacBook Pro could adopt an iPhone-like Dynamic Island interface built around the camera cutout.

The touchscreen MacBook Pro is also expected to retain its traditional laptop design, complete with a full keyboard and large trackpad, rather than becoming a hybrid tablet device.

Other rumoured design changes include:

  • A thinner and lighter chassis.
  • OLED display technology.
  • A hole-punch FaceTime camera replacing the notch.
  • Possible Dynamic Island-style functionality.
  • A reinforced hinge designed to minimise screen movement when the display is touched.

These changes would help distinguish the MacBook Pro from the MacBook Air and the entry-level MacBook Neo while giving Apple’s flagship laptop its most substantial design update in years.

Which chip will feature in the touchscreen MacBook?

  • M5 Pro and M5 Max

Early rumors suggested that Apple’s first touchscreen MacBook Pro would feature M6 Pro and M6 Max chips, but more recent reports indicate that Apple has changed its plans. The redesigned OLED models are now expected to launch with M5 Pro and M5 Max processors, with Apple potentially skipping the M6 Pro and M6 Max generation entirely.

According to Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman in June 2026, Apple has revised its chip roadmap to accelerate development of the AI-focused M7 generation. The change could bring the M7 chips to market around six months earlier, with significantly improved on-device AI capabilities. Apple has taken its sweet time to make a smart display – just as it didn’t rush to make a folding phone. Google and Amazon have been in the smart display business for the best part of a decade, while Apple fans have been watching from the sidelines, with a HomePod in the corner of their kitchen and an iPad propped against the toaster. 

I’ll admit that when I first heard the rumours about Apple’s smart display, I expected the final product to look like an original HomePod speaker with a screen bolted on. But within a few minutes of seeing HomeView at Apple’s Home event in New York, I was smiling. It’s a charming little device that’s both a household device and a personalized one, something you can’t say about the single-user iPad. There are a couple of things to note about HomeView, which I’ll get to, but there’s a lot to love.

Cute and compact

HomeView is cute. That might not be the most eloquent adjective, but it’s the best way to describe how I felt when seeing it for the first time. A 7-inch LCD screen floats above a rounded aluminium base on a stainless-steel hinge, and you can nudge the display back or forward depending on whether it’s on a low nightstand or a tall counter.

The hinge is a joy, too. It has firm, satisfying resistance, so the screen moves when you want it to and stays put when you let go – not too dissimilar to how I felt about the iPhone Duo when I tried it last month. It feels high-end in the way Apple hardware usually does, with no creaking, no plastic pretending to be metal, and a premium, solid feel all over.

Foundry

There are four color options—Silver, Starlight, Rose Pink, and Space Gray—and Apple matches the USB-C cable to the body, similar to the iMac and its accessories. They’re muted shades that will blend well with whatever’s around it: wood, tile, or painted walls. Starlight was my favorite of the four, with its warm, soft tone, but they’re all lovely. 

The device itself includes a several rows of holes on the base and under the display for speakers, which pack two full-range drivers into the display, plus a down-firing woofer and two passive radiators in the base. It looks more like a Dyson appliance than an Apple gadget, but it sounds great for something so compact. Think somewhere between a HomePod mini and the full-size HomePod: noticeably fuller and punchier than the mini, without quite the room-filling presence of its big sibling.

If you’d rather put a HomeView in a hallway or on the kitchen wall, there’s a wall-mounted version too, which is only available in Silver or Space Gray. That model has the same aluminium display frame, but without the speaker base, the sound quality won’t be as good, so that’s something to consider.

Shared yet personalized

HomeView can do a lot, but the feature I appreciated most was face recognition. HomeView can learn up to six faces within a household, and once it recognises you, a swipe up from the bottom of the screen brings up a home screen that is not only familiar but personalised, too.

Your calendar, reminders, messages and widgets will all appear, along with the design customisations you’ve made, such as coloured or clear app icons. If someone else comes into the frame, HomeView will ask whether you want to switch profiles, and if you do, their home screen will then appear seamlessly. 

Foundry

It’s a smart way to work around the problem with shared screens. A kitchen display is a family device, but it’s helpful to have personal content, and HomeView manages to be both. It is worth noting that to show personal information like calendars and messages, the person not only needs to be recognised, but their iPhone also needs to be close by and “recently” unlocked.

Handoff was also impressive, and it’s another area where being an Apple household will really pay off. In my demo, an iPhone was held next to the HomeView screen with a recipe open in Safari, and it carried over to HomeView without hesitation. FaceTime calls jump across the same way, as does media, so it looks like it will be lovely and simple to start something on your iPhone and move it over to the bigger HomeView display.

Jumping back to recipes for a second, though, as this was a standout feature and a good indication of how Apple expects it will be used. Open a recipe in Safari on the HomeView display (or hand one off from your iPhone), and it will automatically pull out the ingredients and instructions. Tap “Start Cooking,” and HomeView will then present you with a single step at a time, allowing you to swipe through to the next when ready.

It handles timers well, too, picking out the cooking times buried in each step and starting a timer immediately if you tap on it. You can set multiple timers, and they appear at the top of the HomeView display. It works much like Dynamic Island, though tapping it expands the timer to the full screen rather than an expanded view like on the iPhone.

Foundry

At the heart of HomeView is Apple’s new Siri AI, which can finally hold a conversation, follow up on previous queries, and answer questions that would previously have earned a shrug from the old Siri. With an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone paired, Siri AI can dig into your calendar and messages to use personal context to find things for you, too.

I saw it in a demo, and it worked well (as demos usually do). There’s reason to be optimistic, though—I’ve been impressed with Siri AI over the last few months, and I expect it to be just as good on HomeView.

Guests aren’t left out either, but if your visitors have an Android phone, the experience won’t be anywhere near as rich or polished as those baked into the Apple ecosystem (no surprises there). Anyone without an Apple Account can still use HomeView, and the owner can select what they get access to in guest mode, such as playing music, browsing shared photos, or turning on the lights, while keeping everyone’s personal stuff locked away. There’s also a feature that uses the front camera to show you what you look like, in case you don’t feel like looking in a mirror. 

A couple of considerations

There are a couple of elements that take some of the shine off, though. HomeView works with accessories that support Apple Home or Matter, including Apple’s new Home Collection of cameras, thermostats, and a lock. That’s a lot of newer smart home products, but it’s far from everything. Many popular smart home brands, such as Ring, don’t support either, and if your setup leans on them, HomeView’s dashboard may end up with a few gaps where your gear should be.

Foundry

Apple would clearly love you to build your home around its ecosystem from day one, and that’s fine if you’re starting fresh. If you’ve spent years piecing together a mixed setup, though, HomeView leaves you with two options: live with the gaps or start replacing things. For example, the Home Camera face can stream up to nine camera feeds at once, which is great, but only if your cameras make the cut. If you’re considering the HomeView primarily as a smart home hub, my advice would be to check what you already own against Apple’s compatibility list before you pre-order.

The built-in camera has its own limits, too. It’s a 12MP sensor with Center Stage, so it does a great job of keeping you in frame on FaceTime, even as you shuffle around the kitchen. Unlike Google’s Nest Hub Max, though, it can’t act as a security camera or allow you to “Drop In” on your home, as you can with Amazon’s Echo Show devices. HomeView can work as an intercom, but it doesn’t offer anything with video like either of those.

Foundry

Finally, while the lovely square screen has plenty going for it, it isn’t going to be great for watching video. The shape makes it stand out from rivals, and it suits album art, photos, and recipes perfectly, but it works against watching a quick TV show or recipe on YouTube while cooking. Instead, you’ll get thick bars above and below, which would be bearable for keeping an eye on a game while you cook, but if you want to actually watch something properly in the kitchen, propping that iPad back up against the toaster will do a much better job.

Last but not least, there’s no physical privacy switch. Apple processes camera and microphone data within the A18’s Secure Enclave, which neither the software nor Apple can access, according to the company. However, some users will likely still want a way to shut off the camera and microphones physically, as competitors offer, rather than relying solely on software toggles. 

Is HomeView worth a $299 pre-order?

Apple HomeView costs $299, with the wall-mounted model priced the same. The catch with the wall version is that the mounts are sold separately, starting at $59.95 for the USB-C plug-in option, $79.95 for the AC-wired option, and $129.95 for a Power over Ethernet mount that will arrive in early 2027. Hanging one in your hallway, then, costs closer to $360 or more, plus any additional costs for installation. And for some reason, it doesn’t come with a power adapter like the base model. 

Foundry

For the tabletop model, $299 feels fair if you live in Apple’s world. You’re getting a great speaker, a gorgeous screen, a decent FaceTime camera, Siri AI, and both a shared and a personalised hub that will look great in any room. It’s also the cheapest way to access Siri AI. There are some things to consider, such as support for existing smart home products you have and whether you mind the lack of a privacy switch. I’ll need to test it fully to see how it responds to my world and my family, but from what I’ve seen so far, HomeView seems set to slot right into my home.

Apple’s HomeView arrives on November 13, and preorders are open now on Apple.com, Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers.

Tap “Start Cooking,” and HomeView will then present you with a single step at a time, allowing you to swipe through to the next when ready.

It handles timers well, too, picking out the cooking times buried in each step and starting a timer immediately if you tap on it. You can set multiple timers, and they appear at the top of the HomeView display. It works much like Dynamic Island, though tapping it expands the timer to the full screen rather than an expanded view like on the iPhone.

Foundry

At the heart of HomeView is Apple’s new Siri AI, which can finally hold a conversation, follow up on previous queries, and answer questions that would previously have earned a shrug from the old Siri. With an Apple Intelligence-capable iPhone paired, Siri AI can dig into your calendar and messages to use personal context to find things for you, too.

I saw it in a demo, and it worked well (as demos usually do). There’s reason to be optimistic, though—I’ve been impressed with Siri AI over the last few months, and I expect it to be just as good on HomeView.

Guests aren’t left out either, but if your visitors have an Android phone, the experience won’t be anywhere near as rich or polished as those baked into the Apple ecosystem (no surprises there). Anyone without an Apple Account can still use HomeView, and the owner can select what they get access to in guest mode, such as playing music, browsing shared photos, or turning on the lights, while keeping everyone’s personal stuff locked away. There’s also a feature that uses the front camera to show you what you look like, in case you don’t feel like looking in a mirror. 

A couple of considerations

There are a couple of elements that take some of the shine off, though. HomeView works with accessories that support Apple Home or Matter, including Apple’s new Home Collection of cameras, thermostats, and a lock. That’s a lot of newer smart home products, but it’s far from everything. Many popular smart home brands, such as Ring, don’t support either, and if your setup leans on them, HomeView’s dashboard may end up with a few gaps where your gear should be.

Foundry

Apple would clearly love you to build your home around its ecosystem from day one, and that’s fine if you’re starting fresh. If you’ve spent years piecing together a mixed setup, though, HomeView leaves you with two options: live with the gaps or start replacing things. For example, the Home Camera face can stream up to nine camera feeds at once, which is great, but only if your cameras make the cut. If you’re considering the HomeView primarily as a smart home hub, my advice would be to check what you already own against Apple’s compatibility list before you pre-order.

The built-in camera has its own limits, too. It’s a 12MP sensor with Center Stage, so it does a great job of keeping you in frame on FaceTime, even as you shuffle around the kitchen. Unlike Google’s Nest Hub Max, though, it can’t act as a security camera or allow you to “Drop In” on your home, as you can with Amazon’s Echo Show devices. HomeView can work as an intercom, but it doesn’t offer anything with video like either of those.

Foundry

Finally, while the lovely square screen has plenty going for it, it isn’t going to be great for watching video. The shape makes it stand out from rivals, and it suits album art, photos, and recipes perfectly, but it works against watching a quick TV show or recipe on YouTube while cooking. Instead, you’ll get thick bars above and below, which would be bearable for keeping an eye on a game while you cook, but if you want to actually watch something properly in the kitchen, propping that iPad back up against the toaster will do a much better job.

Last but not least, there’s no physical privacy switch. Apple processes camera and microphone data within the A18’s Secure Enclave, which neither the software nor Apple can access, according to the company. However, some users will likely still want a way to shut off the camera and microphones physically, as competitors offer, rather than relying solely on software toggles. 

Is HomeView worth a $299 pre-order?

Apple HomeView costs $299, with the wall-mounted model priced the same. The catch with the wall version is that the mounts are sold separately, starting at $59.95 for the USB-C plug-in option, $79.95 for the AC-wired option, and $129.95 for a Power over Ethernet mount that will arrive in early 2027. Hanging one in your hallway, then, costs closer to $360 or more, plus any additional costs for installation. And for some reason, it doesn’t come with a power adapter like the base model. 

Foundry

For the tabletop model, $299 feels fair if you live in Apple’s world. You’re getting a great speaker, a gorgeous screen, a decent FaceTime camera, Siri AI, and both a shared and a personalised hub that will look great in any room. It’s also the cheapest way to access Siri AI. There are some things to consider, such as support for existing smart home products you have and whether you mind the lack of a privacy switch. I’ll need to test it fully to see how it responds to my world and my family, but from what I’ve seen so far, HomeView seems set to slot right into my home.

Apple’s HomeView arrives on November 13, and preorders are open now on Apple.com, Amazon, Best Buy, and other retailers.

Apple has unveiled the HomePod mini 2, the first major update to its smallest smart speaker since the original launched in November 2020. Announced on October 13, 2026, the new HomePod mini brings Apple’s more capable Siri AI assistant, upgraded audio experiences, improved connectivity, and a selection of new colors. It retains the familiar compact, spherical design but features significantly improved technology inside.

The biggest upgrade is Siri AI, which will bring more natural conversations, broader knowledge, and greater awareness of personal information stored on connected Apple devices. This will allow users to ask more complex questions, find information in messages and emails, and perform tasks across apps. Siri AI will arrive in a future software update. To enable it, the owner of the home in the Home app needs an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone or iPad with current software and Siri AI enabled in a supported language. Other household members can then use its general conversational features without their own compatible device, but personal-context requests require a paired Apple Intelligence-enabled device.

Apple has also replaced the original HomePod mini’s aging S5 processor with the newer S10 chip, enabling enhanced computational audio. Other major additions include four-speaker surround sound when paired with the fourth-generation Apple TV 4K, the ability to use HomePod mini 2 as the default audio output for a Mac equipped with Wi-Fi 6E or later, and Sound Glow, which turns the illuminated touch surface into a colorful display that responds to music. Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6 bring the speaker’s wireless technology up to date.

The HomePod mini 2 comes in five colors: pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. It costs $149, compared with the previous model’s $129 price following Apple’s June 2026 price increase. Pre-orders opened on October 13, with the new speaker going on sale on Friday, October 30. It’s a substantial upgrade for anyone buying their first HomePod mini, although existing owners may find the strongest reason to upgrade is the new Siri experience.

HomePod mini 2 vs. HomePod mini: The 10 biggest changes

The biggest improvements are in software intelligence, audio capabilities, and wireless connectivity rather than the speaker’s physical design. Its fundamental audio hardware remains familiar, including the full-range driver, dual passive radiators, and 360-degree acoustic waveguide.

HomePod mini 2 release date: When will it go on sale?

Apple announced the HomePod mini 2 on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, at its “Welcome Home” product launch. The new speaker is available to pre-order immediately, with the official release date set for Friday, October 30, 2026.

Customers in the U.S. and more than 23 other countries and regions can order the HomePod mini 2 through the Apple online store or Apple Store app. It will also be available in Apple retail stores from October 30. Other retailers are expected to stock the speaker, although Apple hasn’t provided a confirmed list of third-party sellers.

The new model arrives almost six years after the original HomePod mini launched in November 2020. Apple had been widely expected to update the speaker in 2025, but reports suggested that development of its redesigned Siri assistant delayed the launch. Although the new hardware is finally arriving, customers will still have to wait for a subsequent software update before they can use Siri AI.

Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.S.

Pre-order the HomePod mini 2 from Apple U.K.

HomePod mini 2 design: What does it look like?

Apple

Apple hasn’t radically redesigned the HomePod mini for its second generation. The new speaker retains the familiar spherical shape, with a seamless acoustic mesh covering its body and an illuminated touch-sensitive surface on top. It’s designed to fit unobtrusively on a desk, bookshelf, kitchen counter, or bedside table.

The HomePod mini 2 measures 3.3 inches (84.3mm) high and 3.9 inches (97.9mm) wide, exactly the same dimensions as its predecessor. It weighs 335g, making it slightly lighter than the original 345g model. Apple continues to use acoustically transparent fabric, allowing sound to travel through the enclosure in every direction.

The most obvious visual changes are the colors. HomePod mini 2 is available in pink, green, blue, white, and midnight. Pink and green replace the outgoing orange and yellow options, while blue has a darker appearance than before. Interestingly, these colors closely match those revealed in Apple software before the announcement, although a previously rumored red version hasn’t appeared.

The other significant visual upgrade is Sound Glow, which makes the illuminated surface on top much more expressive. Rather than simply displaying Siri’s familiar animations, it can pulse and glow in response to the bass and treble of music. Colors can reflect the artwork of the song being played, while soundscapes such as rain produce their own lighting effects. Voice control element of Sound Glow requires an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone running the latest software.

Apple hasn’t changed the basic touch controls. Users can still tap to play or pause music, double-tap to skip forward, triple-tap to skip backward, touch and hold to activate Siri, and use the illuminated plus and minus controls to adjust volume. The biggest interface improvements therefore come from Sound Glow and the forthcoming Siri AI features rather than new physical buttons.

HomePod mini 2 processor: What chip does it use?

The HomePod mini 2 uses Apple’s S10 chip, replacing the original model’s S5. It powers computational audio that adjusts the sound in real time, including its dynamic range and loudness.

The new model also supports the forthcoming Siri AI features, including more conversational requests and access to personal context. These will arrive through a future software update and require compatible Apple devices.

The redesigned Siri will support more conversational requests, broader world knowledge, and personal context awareness, with processing distributed between the HomePod, connected Apple devices, and Apple’s Private Cloud Compute servers.

HomePod mini 2 connectivity: What’s changed?

Apple

The HomePod mini 2 brings two confirmed wireless upgrades: Wi-Fi 6E and Bluetooth 6. These replace the original model’s older Wi-Fi 4 and Bluetooth 5.0 technologies, bringing the speaker up to date with Apple’s latest wireless ecosystem.

Wi-Fi 6E adds access to the 6GHz wireless band when used with a compatible router, potentially reducing congestion and improving network performance in busy homes. Bluetooth 6 introduces newer wireless capabilities, although Apple hasn’t specified which Bluetooth improvements the HomePod mini 2 takes advantage of.

The new HomePod mini also supports Thread networking, allowing it to act as part of a compatible smart-home network. This helps it communicate with devices such as smart lights, sensors, and other supported accessories without relying exclusively on traditional Wi-Fi connections.

Apple lists an Ultra Wideband chip for device proximity, continuing support for proximity-based interactions with compatible devices. However, the technical specifications don’t identify the generation of the chip, so it isn’t yet possible to confirm whether this is an improvement over the original model’s U1 hardware.

Despite earlier rumors about Apple’s in-house wireless networking technology, the company hasn’t named a specific Apple-designed connectivity chip for the HomePod mini 2. The speaker continues to depend on Wi-Fi for its internet connection.

HomePod mini 2 speaker setup

You can use HomePod mini 2 on its own, pair two for stereo sound, or build a four-speaker surround system with a compatible Apple TV – while supported Macs can use a single speaker or stereo pair.

Can you use HomePod mini 2 speakers for stereo or surround sound?

You can use one HomePod mini 2 on its own or combine two into a stereo pair, with separate left and right audio channels. Stereo pairing was available on the original HomePod mini.

The new addition is four-speaker surround sound with an Apple TV 4K (4th generation) running the latest software. This uses two speakers at the front and two at the rear.

Each pair must contain matching models, but the front and rear pairs can differ. For example, you can use two HomePod (2nd generation) speakers at the front and two HomePod mini 2 speakers at the rear.

Which Macs can use HomePod mini 2 as their default speaker?

HomePod mini 2 can serve as the default audio output for a Mac with Wi-Fi 6E or later. You can use one speaker or two HomePod mini 2 speakers configured as a stereo pair. Four-speaker surround sound requires an Apple TV 4K (4th generation) and isn’t supported through this Mac feature.

Compatible models include:

  • Mac mini: M2 and M2 Pro models or newer
  • MacBook Pro: 14-inch and 16-inch models introduced in 2023 or later
  • Mac Studio: M2 Max and M2 Ultra models or newer
  • Mac Pro: M2 Ultra model
  • iMac: M3 models or newer
  • MacBook Air: M3 models or newer

HomePod mini 2 price: How much does it cost?

The HomePod mini 2 costs $149/£149, making it $20/£20 more expensive than the previous-generation model at its most recent official price. It’s also $50/£50 more expensive than the original HomePod mini was when it launched in November 2020.

Apple initially sold the HomePod mini for $99/£99, but increased the price to $129/£129 in June 2026. The new model therefore represents another price increase, although it brings a significantly newer processor, support for Siri AI, improved connectivity, and additional audio capabilities.

A 20W power adapter is included in both the U.S. and U.K. boxes. Apple lists an iPhone or iPad running the latest iOS or iPadOS, plus Wi-Fi internet access, as requirements for using the speaker.

Should you buy a HomePod mini 2?

The HomePod mini 2 looks like a worthwhile purchase for anyone looking for an affordable Apple smart speaker, particularly those interested in Siri AI, smart-home control, new Mac audio and home theater options. The S10 chip, upgraded connectivity, and new audio features make it a much more capable device than its predecessor.

However, existing HomePod mini owners shouldn’t rush to upgrade. The design and fundamental speaker hardware remain largely unchanged, and Siri AI won’t arrive until a future software update. If you mainly use your HomePod for music, an inexpensive first-generation model could still be a good choice. For more powerful sound, consider the full-size HomePod.

You waited months for Apple’s new iPhones to arrive, but it’s worth protecting that big investment from day one. The iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max are tougher than previous generations, but they can still be scratched, chipped or damaged in a drop. A good case also does more than protect your phone: it can improve grip, add a stand or wallet, support MagSafe accessories and give your iPhone a completely different look.

There are thousands of iPhone cases to choose from, ranging from inexpensive silicone shells to rugged cases built for serious drop protection. Price isn’t always a reliable guide to quality, either: a cheap case can split, yellow or develop faulty buttons, while spending more doesn’t necessarily mean you’ll get the best case for your needs.

That’s why we hand-test and compare as many iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max cases as we can. We consider protection, materials, build quality, grip, raised screen and camera edges, MagSafe compatibility, weight, useful extras such as stands and card storage, and how the case feels in everyday use. Where manufacturers make specific drop-protection claims, we include those too so you can compare different levels of protection.

In this guide we’ve grouped our recommendations into clear, colorful, protective and leather or faux-leather cases, with options at a range of prices.

  • Best clear cases for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max
  • Best fun cases for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max
  • Best protective cases for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max
  • Best leather cases for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max
  • Best wallet cases for iPhone 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max

Which type of iPhone case to choose

Apple gives you a handful of finishes; a case gives you thousands—an easy way to make an iPhone 18 Pro look like yours. You can choose a clear case that shows off the iPhone’s original color but adds vital protection, or choose a case with more personality. Protection is key, and some cases will add higher levels of defense than others.

Beyond looks, think about how you use your phone. Want hands-free video? Look for a case with a built-in stand. Want to leave your wallet at home? Choose one with a card storage wallet. And if you charge wirelessly, check for MagSafe compatibility — most cases now offer it, and it’s worth confirming before you buy.

Best clear cases for iPhone 18

If you want to keep your iPhone 18 Pro or iPhone 18 Pro Max looking like Apple intended you could leave it unprotected without a case, or simply choose a clear case that shows off the iPhone’s color while protecting it from everyday knocks and drops.

Best protective cases for iPhone 18

As pretty as some iPhone cases are, your principal consideration should be protection. Most decent cases offer reasonable protection, but these protective cases have extra robust features while often adding as little bulk as possible by using the latest, strongest materials. Kevlar is the material used to make bulletproof vests—it’s also known as Aramid Fiber—but I wouldn’t try turning a rifle on it. Graphene is even stronger, and would probably make Superman wince trying to snap it in half.

Other protective iPhone cases don’t worry so much about thinness, and bulk up to protect your iPhone from the worst disasters that can befall it. These might suit you if you work in riskier environments or are an active outdoors iPhone user.

Material matters too: Graphene (elastic yet harder than diamond and up to 200x stronger than steel, according to case makers) or Kevlar (the material used to make bulletproof vests) for serious durability. Kevlar is a type of Aramid Fiber, a strong, heat-resistant synthetic material that gives the material incredible strength and stability.

FAQ

1.

What is Apple’s Ceramic Shield protection for iPhones?

Apple introduced Ceramic Shield with the iPhone 12 in 2020, developed jointly with glassmaker Corning, and it’s been standard on every iPhone since (excluding the budget SE line).

It’s made by fusing nano-ceramic crystals into glass, then dipping it in molten salt so potassium ions swap places with smaller sodium ions, creating a compressive surface layer that resists cracking. This gave the original iPhone 12 four times better drop performance than the iPhone 11.

Ceramic Shield 2 arrived with the iPhone 17 lineup in 2025, keeping the same crystal-infusion and ion-exchange process but with a refined composition that’s roughly three times more scratch-resistant than the first generation, while retaining similar drop protection. On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Ceramic Shield 2 protects the front, while the back uses Ceramic Shield.

2.

Why do you need an iPhone case?

Your iPhone is a precision device that lives in an unpredictable world—pockets, bags, countertops, pavement. A case is what stands between an accidental drop and a cracked screen or shattered back. It’s not a small risk either: plenty of new iPhone owners crack a screen within the first ten weeks of ownership (source). The IP68 rating means real dust and water resistance, but that’s a lab result—real life is messier. Add in the daily wear of being pulled in and out of a pocket, plus UV exposure over time, and the damage adds up quietly. A case won’t make your iPhone indestructible, but it absorbs the everyday hits so you don’t end up paying for a repair — or a replacement.

3.

Will the iPhone 18 Pro fit a case for the iPhone 17 Pro?

The iPhone 18 Pro series are virtually identical to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. Even my iPhone 16 Pro fits in an 18 Pro case, and it works just fine—it looks a bit weird at the back, but otherwise fits nicely. On the other hand, a 17 Pro or 18 Pro wouldn’t fit in a 16 Pro case because of the rear camera positioning. Rokform told Macworld that its iPhone 18 Pro case lineup is compatible with iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro models. However, its older iPhone 17 Pro case lineup is not compatible with iPhone 18 models due to camera plateau design differences. Cases designed with tight tolerances might therefore have a problem as the camera plateau on iPhone 18 Pro/Max is about 0.5mm taller than on iPhone 17 Pro/Max.

Leading case manufacturer OtterBox reports that its iPhone 18 Pro/Max cases are “also compatible with iPhone 17 Pro, so the cases can be used interchangeably between those two models”.

New cases are custom-built for each device to guarantee a perfect fit and protection, so buying a case built specifically for your iPhone model is the safest option. Check our roundup of the Best iPhone 17 Cases and Best iPhone 16 Cases for the older models.

4.

Do I need a screen protector if I use a case?

Yes, it’s still worth using a screen protector even if you have a case, as the two provide different but complementary protection. A case protects the back, corners, and edges of your iPhone, while a screen protector is designed to protect the display itself from scratches and cracks.

Tempered-glass screen protectors can help absorb direct impacts and protect against everyday scratches and abrasions. A case with a raised screen lip offers some protection if your iPhone lands face down, but it can’t prevent every object or surface from making direct contact with the screen.

5.

What type of iPhone case offers the best protection?

When it comes to maximum protection for your iPhone, the clear winners are rugged cases built with multi-layer materials and military-grade drop ratings. Rugged cases typically combine a hard polycarbonate outer shell with a shock-absorbing TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) inner layer, reinforced corners, and raised edges around both the screen and camera to prevent direct surface contact on drops.

While silicone and leather cases offer decent everyday scratch protection, they simply can’t match the impact resistance of a purpose-built rugged case.

When choosing a protective case, look for:

  • Raised screen edge around the front (at least 1mm) to keep the screen safely off surfaces.
  • Raised camera edge (0.5mm minimum, some go up to 3.6mm).
  • MIL-STD-810G certification — a U.S. Department of Defense standard for durability.
  • Reinforced corners for impact absorption.
  • MagSafe compatibility if you wirelessly charge.
6.

Do I need an iPhone case for iPhone 18?

Many consumers damage their devices each year, with cracked, chipped or shattered screens the leading reason for iPhone repairs. A screen protector is an important first line of defense, but a case with a raised screen edge can much better protect the display from everyday knocks and drops, and tough sides and back will reduce the risk of damage from an accidental fall.

Ceramic Shield 2, introduced with the iPhone 17 generation, protects the front of the iPhone 18 Pro and offers three times better scratch resistance than the iPhone 16 Pro. The back uses Ceramic Shield, which Apple says offers four times better crack resistance than the back glass used on earlier models.

The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are the best-protected iPhones yet, but a case is still worth buying. It helps keep that pristine finish looking new and, when it’s time to trade up, a well-protected iPhone can retain far more resale value than the cost of the case itself.

Most decent cases offer reasonable protection, but these protective cases have extra robust features while often adding as little bulk as possible by using the latest, strongest materials. Kevlar is the material used to make bulletproof vests—it’s also known as Aramid Fiber—but I wouldn’t try turning a rifle on it. Graphene is even stronger, and would probably make Superman wince trying to snap it in half.

Other protective iPhone cases don’t worry so much about thinness, and bulk up to protect your iPhone from the worst disasters that can befall it. These might suit you if you work in riskier environments or are an active outdoors iPhone user.

Material matters too: Graphene (elastic yet harder than diamond and up to 200x stronger than steel, according to case makers) or Kevlar (the material used to make bulletproof vests) for serious durability. Kevlar is a type of Aramid Fiber, a strong, heat-resistant synthetic material that gives the material incredible strength and stability.

FAQ

1.

What is Apple’s Ceramic Shield protection for iPhones?

Apple introduced Ceramic Shield with the iPhone 12 in 2020, developed jointly with glassmaker Corning, and it’s been standard on every iPhone since (excluding the budget SE line).

It’s made by fusing nano-ceramic crystals into glass, then dipping it in molten salt so potassium ions swap places with smaller sodium ions, creating a compressive surface layer that resists cracking. This gave the original iPhone 12 four times better drop performance than the iPhone 11.

Ceramic Shield 2 arrived with the iPhone 17 lineup in 2025, keeping the same crystal-infusion and ion-exchange process but with a refined composition that’s roughly three times more scratch-resistant than the first generation, while retaining similar drop protection. On the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, Ceramic Shield 2 protects the front, while the back uses Ceramic Shield.

2.

Why do you need an iPhone case?

Your iPhone is a precision device that lives in an unpredictable world—pockets, bags, countertops, pavement. A case is what stands between an accidental drop and a cracked screen or shattered back. It’s not a small risk either: plenty of new iPhone owners crack a screen within the first ten weeks of ownership (source). The IP68 rating means real dust and water resistance, but that’s a lab result—real life is messier. Add in the daily wear of being pulled in and out of a pocket, plus UV exposure over time, and the damage adds up quietly. A case won’t make your iPhone indestructible, but it absorbs the everyday hits so you don’t end up paying for a repair — or a replacement.

3.

Will the iPhone 18 Pro fit a case for the iPhone 17 Pro?

The iPhone 18 Pro series are virtually identical to the iPhone 17 Pro and Pro Max. Even my iPhone 16 Pro fits in an 18 Pro case, and it works just fine—it looks a bit weird at the back, but otherwise fits nicely. On the other hand, a 17 Pro or 18 Pro wouldn’t fit in a 16 Pro case because of the rear camera positioning. Rokform told Macworld that its iPhone 18 Pro case lineup is compatible with iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 17 Pro models. However, its older iPhone 17 Pro case lineup is not compatible with iPhone 18 models due to camera plateau design differences. Cases designed with tight tolerances might therefore have a problem as the camera plateau on iPhone 18 Pro/Max is about 0.5mm taller than on iPhone 17 Pro/Max.

Leading case manufacturer OtterBox reports that its iPhone 18 Pro/Max cases are “also compatible with iPhone 17 Pro, so the cases can be used interchangeably between those two models”.

New cases are custom-built for each device to guarantee a perfect fit and protection, so buying a case built specifically for your iPhone model is the safest option. Check our roundup of the Best iPhone 17 Cases and Best iPhone 16 Cases for the older models.

4.

Do I need a screen protector if I use a case?

Yes, it’s still worth using a screen protector even if you have a case, as the two provide different but complementary protection. A case protects the back, corners, and edges of your iPhone, while a screen protector is designed to protect the display itself from scratches and cracks.

Tempered-glass screen protectors can help absorb direct impacts and protect against everyday scratches and abrasions. A case with a raised screen lip offers some protection if your iPhone lands face down, but it can’t prevent every object or surface from making direct contact with the screen.

5.

What type of iPhone case offers the best protection?

When it comes to maximum protection for your iPhone, the clear winners are rugged cases built with multi-layer materials and military-grade drop ratings. Rugged cases typically combine a hard polycarbonate outer shell with a shock-absorbing TPU (thermoplastic polyurethane) inner layer, reinforced corners, and raised edges around both the screen and camera to prevent direct surface contact on drops.

While silicone and leather cases offer decent everyday scratch protection, they simply can’t match the impact resistance of a purpose-built rugged case.

When choosing a protective case, look for:

  • Raised screen edge around the front (at least 1mm) to keep the screen safely off surfaces.
  • Raised camera edge (0.5mm minimum, some go up to 3.6mm).
  • MIL-STD-810G certification — a U.S. Department of Defense standard for durability.
  • Reinforced corners for impact absorption.
  • MagSafe compatibility if you wirelessly charge.
6.

Do I need an iPhone case for iPhone 18?

Many consumers damage their devices each year, with cracked, chipped or shattered screens the leading reason for iPhone repairs. A screen protector is an important first line of defense, but a case with a raised screen edge can much better protect the display from everyday knocks and drops, and tough sides and back will reduce the risk of damage from an accidental fall.

Ceramic Shield 2, introduced with the iPhone 17 generation, protects the front of the iPhone 18 Pro and offers three times better scratch resistance than the iPhone 16 Pro. The back uses Ceramic Shield, which Apple says offers four times better crack resistance than the back glass used on earlier models.

The 18 Pro and 18 Pro Max are the best-protected iPhones yet, but a case is still worth buying. It helps keep that pristine finish looking new and, when it’s time to trade up, a well-protected iPhone can retain far more resale value than the cost of the case itself.

How we test iPhone cases

When we receive new cases, we test them for fit, button feel, grip, MagSafe strength and alignment, raised-edge camera and screen protection, bulk, weight, and day-to-day handling. Where we are unable to test a case ourselves, we assess it based on its specifications and our experience with other cases from the same manufacturer that have impressed us. We report manufacturers’ claimed drop-protection metrics. As we have listed iPhone cases only from trusted companies we feel safe in these claims but note that measurement is the maker’s own and not ours or Apple’s.

The iPhone Duo, Apple’s first foldable iPhone, will be available to pre-order on October 16 and goes on sale October 23. Apple’s “Get Ready” process is already open, allowing buyers to choose their configuration and prepare payment, trade-in and delivery details before orders officially open. Pre-orders begin at 5 a.m. Pacific / 8 a.m. Eastern / 1 p.m. BST on Friday October 16.

The Duo opens like a book from a compact 5.4-inch phone into a much larger 7.6-inch device. Apple describes the internal screen as its largest-ever iPhone display, with 50 percent more screen area than the iPhone 18 Pro Max, while the outer display provides more than 90 percent of the screen area of an iPhone 18 Pro.

The biggest change is obviously the folding design, but Apple has done more than simply add a hinge. The iPhone Duo will ship with iOS 27.1, which adapts to different positions and orientations with fold-specific interface and multitasking features. These include Split View, hands-free FaceTime and video, StandBy without charging, and layouts that move seamlessly between the two screens. Apple Pencil USB-C support is also coming later in 2026.

The other major changes are the 7.6-inch nano-texture inner display, Touch ID replacing Face ID, an A20 Pro processor with vapor-chamber cooling, and a dual-battery system designed around the two halves of the phone. Apple has also introduced camera features that exploit the second screen, including Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and Duo FaceTime.

Much of the pre-launch reporting proved accurate: the Duo name, book-style design, roughly 7.7- and 5.4-inch screens, Touch ID, two 48MP rear cameras, two front-facing cameras, A20 Pro, C2 modem, MagSafe and the white/dark-blue colours were all anticipated.

iPhone Duo at a glance

  • Apple’s first folding iPhone, with 5.4-inch outer and 7.6-inch inner displays.
  • Touch ID replaces Face ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button.
  • A20 Pro with vapor-chamber cooling, including a new 2nm manufacturing process.
  • Dual-battery architecture, giving up to 44 hours of video playback on the outer display.
  • Fold-specific iOS and camera features, including Split View, Duo Preview, Smart Take, Kid Cue and hands-free use.

iPhone Duo: Top 10 features

iPhone Duo release date: When will it go on sale?

Apple unveiled the iPhone Duo on September 9, 2026, but unlike the iPhone 18 Pro models it won’t arrive until October.

On Monday, October 12, Apple began to let customers “Get Ready” for iPhone Duo pre-orders. Through the Apple Store app or Apple Store online, buyers are able to choose their preferred color and storage capacity, select a carrier, arrange a trade-in or financing, choose AppleCare+, and enter payment and delivery information in advance. That should make placing the final order considerably quicker once pre-orders open at 5 a.m. Pacific / 8 a.m. Eastern / 1 p.m. BST on Friday October 16.

Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.S.

Pre-order iPhone Duo at Apple U.K.

To get ready to pre-order the iPhone Duo choose the specifications you require and then click on the blue ‘Get ready for pre-order’ button.

Foundry

The iPhone Duo officially goes on sale one week later on Friday, October 23, in more than 70 countries and regions, including the U.S., U.K., Canada, Australia, China, France, Germany, India and Japan. A further 28 countries and regions will get it on October 30.

It will be available directly from Apple online and through Apple Stores, with carrier availability varying by market.

Initial supplies may be limited. A late-September supply-chain report claimed Apple and its manufacturing partners were still experiencing relatively low production yields for the new folding design.

iPhone Duo design: What does it look like?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses a book-style folding design. Closed, it is unusually short and wide for an iPhone, measuring 84.1mm wide, 117.8mm tall and 11.3mm thick. Open it and the width expands to 164.6mm, while thickness reduces to just 5.2mm, making it Apple’s thinnest iPhone when unfolded (taking that mantle from the iPhone Air). It weighs 254g.

The outer screen measures 5.4 inches, while the folding inner panel measures 7.6 inches. Both are Super Retina XDR OLED displays with ProMotion up to 120Hz, Always-On display support and up to 3,000 nits outdoor peak brightness. The internal display also has a nano-texture surface designed to reduce reflections and make the crease less noticeable. The inner display also has a replaceable top cover layer. AppleCare+ lists replacement at $19, although it must be replaced by Apple rather than peeled off like a conventional screen protector. Apple has not yet published the price without AppleCare+.

The frame and hinge cover are made from Grade 5 titanium. Apple uses a mirror-polished finish on the enclosure and a micro-blasted finish on the 3D-printed hinge cover. Ceramic Shield protects the rear, while Ceramic Shield 2 protects the outer display. The phone retains an IP68 rating despite its folding construction.

Apple

There are just two colors: Star White and Night Sky, essentially confirming the pre-event reports of silver/white and a very dark blue. For more information read about the iPhone Duo colors.

Action button and Camera Control

There is Camera Control, giving access to exposure, depth, zoom, cameras, styles and tone. It can also launch the new Siri Camera mode.

However, Apple’s Duo doesn’t feature an Action button. The regular iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max retain both the Action button and Camera Control, so this is one hardware-control compromise of the folding model.

Accessories

Apple is also launching two dedicated accessories for the foldable:

  • The iPhone Duo Case at $79/£79
  • The Duo Folio with Kickstand at $129/£129

Both will be orderable from October 16.

Face ID, Touch ID and the notch

Perhaps the most surprising difference between the iPhone Duo and Apple’s other flagship iPhones is that there is no Face ID.

Instead, Apple has brought back Touch ID, with the fingerprint sensor incorporated into the side button. It works whether the Duo is folded or unfolded, and Apple Watch can also be used to unlock the device. This confirms one of the most persistent pre-launch rumors.

The internal display therefore does not need the TrueDepth sensors used for Face ID. Its FaceTime camera sits beneath the display and disappears when it isn’t being used, giving the inner screen a largely uninterrupted surface.

The inner camera itself is hidden below the display rather than sitting permanently in a visible camera cutout. And yet, despite this and the absence of Face ID, there is still support for Dynamic Island.

iPhone Duo cameras: What cameras does it have?

Apple

The Duo has a 48MP Dual Fusion camera system, comprising:

The Duo does not have variable aperture. Variable aperture is exclusive to the 48MP Fusion Main camera in the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

The biggest camera features for iPhone Duo

Duo Preview

The outer screen can show a live preview while somebody else is being photographed, allowing the subject to adjust their pose and framing.

Smart Take and Kid Cue

Smart Take detects when everybody is ready and automatically captures the shot. Kid Cue uses animations on the outer screen to encourage children to look towards the camera.

Two-screen shooting

The folding design supports unusual shooting configurations, including using the main cameras for selfies or group photos while seeing the composition on the other screen. Duo FaceTime can also put nearby participants onto the outer display.

Other notable camera features include 48MP macro photography, a 2x optical-quality crop from the Main camera, an under-display inner FaceTime camera, Dual Capture for simultaneous front-and-rear video, and 4K Dolby Vision recording at up to 120fps.

Rear cameras

The 48MP Fusion Main has an f/1.6 aperture, sensor-shift stabilization and can shoot 24MP or 48MP images. It also provides a 12MP, 2x optical-quality crop equivalent to a 52mm lens.

The 48MP Fusion Ultra Wide has a 13mm-equivalent lens, f/2.2 aperture and 120-degree field of view. It also supports 48MP macro photography and is the same Ultra Wide camera used by the iPhone 18 Pro family.

That means the Duo does not match the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max camera system. Those phones add a dedicated 48MP Fusion Telephoto and variable aperture on the Main camera, making the Pro models much more flexible for photography despite costing substantially less.

Pre-event reports were divided between a Main + Telephoto and Main + Ultra Wide arrangement. Apple ultimately chose Main + Ultra Wide, confirming the earlier reports that a dedicated telephoto could be sacrificed to save space.

Front cameras

On the outside is a 12MP Center Stage camera with an f/2.2 aperture. It supports Center Stage, automatic portrait/landscape framing, Dual Capture, Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5 and 4K Dolby Vision video at up to 60fps.

Inside is an under-display FaceTime camera with an f/1.8 aperture. Apple does not specify its megapixel resolution. It supports Center Stage for video calls and records at up to 1080p/60fps. Its major advantage is visual rather than photographic: the camera effectively disappears beneath the display when it isn’t being used.

iPhone Duo video features

The Main camera records 4K Dolby Vision at 24, 25, 30, 60, 100 or 120fps, with 4K/120fps also available for slo-mo. Cinematic mode reaches 4K/60fps and Action mode up to 2.8K/60fps. Dual Capture can record at up to 4K/30fps.

Apple’s specifications also do not list ProRes or Apple Log recording for the Duo. Those remain more Pro-oriented capabilities rather than part of Apple’s foldable camera proposition.

The Duo does support Spatial Audio recording, Audio Mix, Dolby Vision HDR and Apple’s computational photography features including Photonic Engine, Deep Fusion, Smart HDR 5, Photographic Styles 3, smart focus tracking and Apple Intelligence-powered editing.

Apple does not list conventional Spatial Video capture in the Duo specifications.

iPhone Duo processor: What processor does it use?

Apple

The iPhone Duo uses the A20 Pro, the same processor as the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max.

It is manufactured using a 2-nanometer process, a major step forward in transistor density and efficiency. Apple combines it with a new chip packaging design inspired by its M-series Mac processors. The package connects the A20 Pro directly to a custom vapor chamber to transfer heat away from the processor more effectively.

The A20 Pro includes:

  • 6-core CPU: two super cores and four efficiency cores
  • 7-core GPU with Neural Accelerators
  • Dual 16-core Neural Engine
  • Hardware-accelerated ray tracing
  • A dedicated display engine capable of operating both Duo displays

Compared with the A19 Pro, Apple says the CPU is up to 20 percent faster, while the GPU is up to 40 percent faster and more power-efficient. The Dual 16-core Neural Engine delivers twice the compute power, while unified-memory bandwidth rises by 50 percent.

Apple also claims that the complete thermal system gives the Duo up to 35 percent better sustained performance than the iPhone 17 Pro. That sustained-performance figure is particularly important for a folding device because prolonged gaming, multitasking and AI workloads generate considerably more heat than short benchmark bursts.

iPhone Duo RAM: How much memory does it have?

Apple has not disclosed how much RAM is inside the iPhone Duo.

Before launch, supply-chain reports consistently pointed to 12GB of RAM, which would make sense given the demands of running two displays, simultaneous applications, Siri AI and larger on-device AI models.

Apple does reveal that A20 Pro has 50 percent more unified-memory bandwidth than A19 Pro, which should help the Duo move data more quickly between the CPU, GPU and Neural Engine.

Extra memory is particularly useful on the Duo because iOS 27.1 can display multiple apps simultaneously and because Apple Intelligence and Siri AI increasingly run generative models locally rather than relying entirely on cloud processing.

iPhone Duo connectivity

Apple

Apple has put a significant amount of its own communications silicon into the iPhone Duo.

It uses Apple’s new C2 cellular modem, replacing Qualcomm silicon. Apple says C2 introduces AI-powered improvements to cellular quality and reliability and supports mmWave 5G in the U.S.

The N1 wireless networking chip provides:

  • Wi-Fi 7 with 2×2 MIMO
  • Bluetooth 6
  • Thread networking

The USB-C port also supports USB 3 data transfers at up to 10Gbps and DisplayPort video output.

The Duo also has Apple’s second-generation Ultra Wideband chip, NFC and precision dual-frequency GPS.

It is eSIM-only worldwide, something that had been widely rumored before launch. Eliminating the SIM tray gives Apple additional internal space for its batteries.

iPhone Handoff – a feature introduced with iOS 27 – makes it easier to use an iPhone Duo alongside another iPhone without needing separate phone numbers. Both devices share your number, with calls, voicemail, messages and Find My location following whichever iPhone you unlock. Only one phone is active at a time. You could use the Duo’s folding display for work, then switch to an iPhone Pro when you want its telephoto camera. Both phones need iOS 27, eSIM support and the same Apple Account, with Messages in iCloud enabled. Your carrier must specifically support iPhone Handoff, and your plan may require an additional monthly fee for access. T-Mobile already offers iPhone Handoff for $5 a month; Verizon and EE (in the U.K.) plan support. Fees may apply.

Satellite capabilities include:

  • Emergency SOS via satellite
  • Roadside Assistance via satellite
  • Find My via satellite
  • Messages via satellite

Battery, MagSafe and charging: What’s available?

Instead of one battery spanning the body, the iPhone Duo contains two rechargeable lithium-ion batteries, with one high-energy battery fitted into each half of the device. Apple’s energy-balancing algorithms make them operate as a single battery system.

Apple rates battery life at:

  • Up to 24 hours of typical use
  • Up to 44 hours video playback using the outer display
  • Up to 31 hours using the inner display
  • Up to 37 hours streamed video on the outer screen
  • Up to 26 hours streamed video on the inner display

Apple has not disclosed the batteries’ combined capacity in mAh. The pre-launch rumor of approximately 5,000-5,500mAh therefore remains unconfirmed.

Apple says the iPhone Duo can reach 50 percent charge in around 20 minutes using a USB-C charging cable and a 60W-capable power adapter or higher.

MagSafe and Qi2 wireless charging are supported at up to 25W. Apple’s claimed 50 percent charge in around 30 minutes requires a MagSafe charger paired with a 35W-or-higher power adapter.

In both the U.S. and U.K., the box includes the iPhone Duo and a 1-meter USB-C charging cable, but no power adapter. The MagSafe charger is also sold separately, so factor these accessories into your budget if you don’t already own suitable equipment.

iPhone Duo price: How much does it cost?

The iPhone Duo starts at $1,999 in the U.S. and £1,999 in the U.K. for 256GB.

Prices are:

The 256GB starting capacity means Apple has not created an unusually low-storage entry model simply to make the headline price look lower.

iPhone Duo vs iPhone 18 Pro pricing

The iPhone 18 Pro starts at $1,199/£1,199, while the iPhone 18 Pro Max starts at $1,299/£1,299. That makes the Duo approximately $700/£700 more expensive than the Pro Max at entry level.

That premium buys the folding display, precision hinge, titanium structure, second screen and more complex dual-battery design rather than superior cameras: in several areas the iPhone 18 Pro models are actually better equipped.

Reports before the launch suggested the Duo could cost anywhere from around $1,999 to $2,399 at entry level, largely because of the folding OLED display, hinge mechanism, titanium components and other expensive parts. Apple ultimately landed at the very bottom of those predictions.

iPhone Duo software: Multitasking and Apple Pencil support

The iPhone Duo’s larger inner display enables Split View, letting you use two apps side by side. For example, you could keep Safari open while taking notes, or check your calendar alongside a conversation in Messages. Supported apps can also open two windows of their own: Safari can display two webpages side by side for comparison shopping. You can save pairs of apps to return to later.

StandBy also works differently on the Duo. Set the phone down and it can display a clock, photos or widgets on either screen without being connected to a charger. New Calendar and Weather faces join the existing options.

Apple Pencil support is coming later in 2026. Apple has announced compatibility with the Apple Pencil (USB-C), allowing users to write, sketch and mark up documents on either display.

Should you buy the iPhone Duo?

The iPhone Duo is the iPhone to buy if you genuinely want a phone and small tablet in one device. Its 7.6-inch display, multitasking features, A20 Pro performance and clever fold-specific camera modes offer capabilities no other iPhone has. 

But at $1,999/£1,999 it is enormously expensive, and there are significant compromises: no Face ID, no dedicated telephoto camera, no variable aperture and no Action button. 

For photography, battery life and conventional everyday use, the iPhone 18 Pro Max is likely to be the better-value flagship. Buy the Duo because you want the folding experience, not because it is simply the “best” iPhone.
